content: Fractures of the femoral shaft in children are rare but significant injuries that can severely impact the lives of both the affected children and their caregivers. These injuries can lead to long-term disabilities if not managed appropriately. Treatment options include surgical interventions, such as intramedullary nailing or external fixation, and conservative approaches, such as prolonged immobilization, often requiring hospitalization. The objective of this study was to evaluate the benefits and harms of various interventions for treating femoral shaft fractures in children and adolescents. The research involved a comprehensive search of multiple databases and sources, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and expert consultations. The search was conducted up to August 2013. The study included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing surgical and conservative treatments for diaphyseal femoral fractures in children under 18 years of age. The primary outcomes assessed were functional outcomes, rates of unacceptable malunion, and serious adverse events. Data were collected and analyzed independently by two authors, and the quality of evidence for each outcome was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 10 trials involving 527 children (531 fractures) were included. All trials had some risk of bias, with only one trial at low risk of selection bias. The overall quality of evidence was judged to be low for most outcomes, indicating uncertainty about the reliability of the findings. Many trials did not report on self-assessed functional outcomes or the time taken for children to resume normal activities. Surgical vs. Conservative Treatment Four trials involving 264 children aged 4 to 12 years compared surgical and conservative treatments. Low-quality evidence from one trial (101 children) showed similar functional outcomes at two years post-treatment, as measured by the RAND health status score (mean scores: 69 for surgery with external fixation vs. 68 for conservative treatment with a spica cast). The other three trials did not report functional outcomes. Moderate-quality evidence from four trials (264 children) indicated that surgery reduced the risk of malunion compared to conservative treatment (risk ratio [RR] 0.29, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.15 to 0.59). This translates to 81 fewer malunions per 1000 children treated surgically, assuming a baseline risk of 115 malunions per 1000 with conservative treatment. Conversely, low-quality evidence suggested that surgery was associated with a higher risk of serious adverse events, such as infections (RR 2.39, 95% CI 1.10 to 5.17). This equates to 56 more serious adverse events per 1000 children treated surgically, assuming a baseline risk of 40 serious adverse events per 1000 with conservative treatment. Low-quality evidence from one trial (101 children) indicated similar levels of satisfaction among children and parents for surgery involving external fixation compared to plaster cast treatment. However, another trial (46 children) suggested that parents were more satisfied with intramedullary nailing than with traction followed by a cast. Surgery also appeared to reduce the time children missed from school. Comparisons of Different Conservative Treatments Three trials evaluated different conservative treatment methods. Very low-quality evidence from one trial (42 children) suggested uncertainty about differences in malunion rates between immediate hip spica casting and skeletal traction followed by spica casting in children aged 3 to 10 years. Another trial (43 children) found no significant difference in malunion rates between traction followed by functional orthosis and traction followed by spica casting in children aged 5 to 13 years. One trial (52 children) compared single-leg and double-leg spica casts. Very low-quality evidence indicated uncertainty about differences in functional outcomes or serious adverse events. However, single-leg spica casts were reported to be less cumbersome for parents, more comfortable for children, and associated with less time off work for caregivers. Comparisons of Different Surgical Treatments Three trials compared different surgical methods. Very low-quality evidence from one trial (19 children) indicated uncertainty about differences in malunion rates, serious adverse events, time to return to school, or parental satisfaction between elastic stable intramedullary nailing and external fixation. Similarly, another trial (52 children) found very low-quality evidence regarding differences in serious adverse events or time to resume full weight-bearing between dynamic and static external fixation. A third trial (47 children) compared intramedullary nailing and submuscular plating. Very low-quality evidence suggested uncertainty about differences in malunion rates, serious adverse events, or time to resume weight-bearing. However, submuscular plating may pose more challenges during plate removal. Authors' Conclusions There is insufficient evidence to determine whether long-term functional outcomes differ between surgical and conservative treatments. Surgery appears to reduce the risk of malunion in children aged 4 to 12 years but may increase the risk of serious adverse events. Elastic stable intramedullary nailing may shorten recovery time. However, there is insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the relative effectiveness of different conservative or surgical treatment methods.
